# Cakkavatti Sutta (DN 26 (PTS DN iii 58))

**ID:** DN 26 (PTS DN iii 58)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cakkavatti Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Wheel-Turning Monarch
**PTS:** DN iii 58
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn26
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cakkavatti Sutta* (also known as the *Cakkavattisīhanāda Sutta*) is the twenty-sixth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983]. Framed around the Buddha's admonition that monastics must dwell as their own island and take the Dhamma as their refuge, the text relates a detailed legendary narrative of past righteous wheel-turning monarchs (*cakkavattin*) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2014]. When a successor king neglects to provide wealth to the impoverished, society falls into systemic poverty, which sequentially triggers theft, violence, moral decline, and decreasing human lifespans [Anālayo 2014; Buddhist Virtues 2011; Radich 2007]. After society plummets into extreme degeneration and violence, a moral turning point initiates a gradual cosmic and physical restoration [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2014]. The discourse is canonical Buddhism's primary locus for the prophecy of the future Buddha Metteyya (Maitreya), who is predicted to appear during the reign of the monarch Saṅkha when the human lifespan reaches 80,000 years [Appleton 2014; Norman 1983; Winternitz 1933; Wallace 2015]. The sutta also includes the canonical teaching that a practitioner who develops the four bases of spiritual power (*iddhipāda*) can live for a full eon (*kappa*) [Radich 2007].

Curated parallels identified by SuttaCentral include DĀ 6 in the Chinese *Dīrghāgama*, MĀ 70 in the *Madhyamāgama*, and Sanskrit fragments catalogued as SHT sutta 62 [SuttaCentral]. Unlike the Chinese versions, the Pali sutta lacks an explicit transition between the introductory advice and the tale, commencing directly with *bhūtapubbaṃ* [Anālayo 2014]. Portions of the narrative, such as the prediction of Maitreya and the palace of King Mahāpanāda, also coincide with passages in the *Divyāvadāna* [Winternitz 1933; Anālayo 2014]. Computational analysis by DharmaNexus confirms strong alignment with the Chinese *Madhyamāgama* (T 26) and matches passages in the Sanskrit *Lalitavistara*, *Yogācārabhūmi*, and *Bhaiṣajyavastu* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records thousands of shared segments across more than 200 texts, showing the densest reuse with the *Tikanipāta* (AN 3), *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta* (MN 129), *Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta* (SN 47), and *Mahāsudassana Sutta* (DN 17) [DharmaNexus].
